prāṇa
(‘that by which one lives’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most widely used words, ‘prāṇa’ has several senses. Some of the उपनिषद्स् like the Kauṣītaki use the word for ब्रह्मन् (2.1). Vedāntic works use the word to denote हिरण्यगर्भ, an aspect of ब्रह्मन्, involved in the process of च्रेअतिओन् through his इच्छाशक्ति or cosmic will-power.
Coming to an individual living being, प्राण is the life-force or vital air, because of which only the being lives. In its primary sense, it is sometimes called mukhyaprāṇa also.
Prāṇa functions inside the body in five different forms. Hence it is also called ‘pañcaprāṇas’.
The five prāṇas are: प्राण, अपान, व्यान, उदान and समान.
Prāṇa is centred in the nose and is responsible for respiration.
Apāna works downwards and is res-ponsible for the working of the excretory organs and the organs of generation.
Vyāna pervades the whole body and supplies the energy necessary for hard work like running or lifting a weight.
Udāna is situated in the throat with its movement poised upwards. It helps the जीव (the individual सोउल्) to leave the body at the time of death.
Samāna, the last of the पञ्चप्राणस्, is situated in the central region of the body and is responsible for digestion or assimilation of ड़ोओद्.
Each of these five prāṇas has a subsidiary called upaprāṇa. The five upaprāṇas are: नाग (of उदान), कूर्म (of व्यान), कृकल (of समान) devadatta (of अपान) and dhanañjaya (of समान). They are responsible for eructation, winking, sneezing, yawning and sustaining the body respectively.
In the उपनिषद्स्, the word is also used to indicate the इन्द्रियस् or senseorgans.

pramāṇas
(‘those which measure,’ ‘valid means of knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
All the six darśanas (Hindu systems of philosophy) accept certain basic sources or means of knowledge, known as ‘pramāṇas’, upon which they further develop their theories.
These प्रमाणस् vary from a minimum of three to a maximum of six. They are as follows.
PRATYAKṢA (direct or immediate perception) has two stages of development. As soon as the sense-organ comes into contact with the sense-object, there is a general awareness of it, as something existing. This is called निर्विकल्पक-प्रत्यक्ष. In the next stage, all the details will be noted in the light of past experience. This is savikalpa-प्रत्यक्ष.
ANUMĀNA (inference) gives us the knowledge of a thing indirectly, when we see some लिङ्ग or sign invariably connected with the original. For instance, by seeing smoke on a yonder hill, we can infer that there is fire there (even though we do not see it directly) since it is known from previous observations and experience that smoke is invariably associated with fire.
UPAMĀNA (comparison) is another source of knowledge. On seeing a rat, one recollects that it is like the mouse he had seen earlier. He then comes to know that the remembered mouse is like the perceived rat. This type of knowledge comes through उपमान.
ŚABDA (verbal testimony) is the next source of knowledge. The मीमाṁसा दर्शन pays the greatest attention to this since it has to justify the undisputed authority of the वेदस्.
The words of a reliable person are believed to be true. This is called āptavākya.
Verbal testimony, however, is of two types: pauruṣeya (personal, same as āptavākya) and apauruṣeya (impersonal). The second denotes the वेदस् since they were not created by any human agency. The वेदस् are supremely authoritative since they are the ‘Book of Commandments’ and also give us authentic know-ledge of the unseen and the unknown truths. Again, their main purport and purpose lies in propagating sacrificial rites.
The वेदस् are eternal, not as the printed Book nor as the orally transmitted mantras but as the eternal teachings contained in them. These teachings are conveyed through the ṛṣis or sages in every age.
Since the वेदस् are mainly concerned with giving commands (= विधि) about the yāgas or sacrificial rites and other associ-ated rituals, only those sentences containing such commands as expressed through the verbs couched in ‘vidhiliṅ’ (imperative mood as in ‘svargakāmo yajeta,’ ‘One desirous of attaining हेअवेन् should sacrifice!’) and other forms should be taken as authoritative and the rest as aids to it. Such verbs have an innate power of urging the hearer to do the sacrifice. This is called ‘bhāvanā’. The urge contained in the Vedic words is known as ‘śābdī-भावना’ (śabda = word). On hearing it, the person who hears it, gets the urge to perform it. This secondary urge is named ‘ārthībhāvanā’ (artha = utility, useful activity).
All this depends upon the correct understanding and interpretation of the Vedic sentences. For this, the Mīmāṁsā gives six steps: उपक्रम (beginning); upasaṁhāra (concluding); अभ्यास (repetition for the sake of emphasis); apūrvatā (not being known earlier by any other means); phala (utility); अर्थवाद (mere eulogy) and upapatti (logic and reasoning).
Once the correct meaning is thus ascertained, the command may be implemented.
ARTHĀPATTI (postulation or presumption) is the necessary supposition of an unperceived fact which alone can explain an anomaly satisfactorily. For instance, if a person is noticed to be getting fat even though he does not eat during the day, it can safely be presumed that he is secretly eating at night! Knowledge obtained by अर्थापत्ति is distinctive since it cannot be got by any other means.
ANUPALABDHI (non-perception) has also been accepted as a source of know-ledge since it gives the immediate चोग्नितिओन् of the non-existence of an object. If it is found that a jar which had been kept on a table earlier, is not perceived now, its non-existence is cognized.

pralaya
(‘dissolution [of the world]’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu scriptures propound the cyclic theory of च्रेअतिओन्. The cycle of सृष्टि (creation), sthiti (preservation) and लय (dissolution) goes on endlessly.
The dissolution, called लय or प्रलय, is of four types: नित्य; naimittika; prākṛtika and ātyantika.
Nityapralaya refers to the daily deaths of beings that are born. Naimittika प्रलय is the dissolution that takes place at the end of a day of ब्रह्मा, called ‘kalpa’ which is equivalent to 4.32 billion human years. The prākṛtika प्रलय is the dissolution of everything into प्रकृति (the basic matrix of the universe, often identified with the māyā-power of God) at the end of ब्रह्मा’s life of (his) hundred years equivalent to 1036 human years. Ātyantikapralaya actually refers to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् wherein a जीव is liberated from transmigratory existence.

prāṇapratiṣṭhā
(‘infusing life [into an image]’)
------------------------------------------
Worship of God through an image is a common aspect of practical हिन्दुइस्म्.
The image, however, whether established in a temple or in one’s होउसे, has first to be infused with life, which process is called ‘prāṇapratiṣṭhā’.
The basic idea is that God who is in one’s own heart, has to be ceremonially transferred to the image and then worshipped.
In the consecration of temples, after several rituals—both major and minor—prāṇapratiṣṭhā is done by uttering the मन्त्र āṁ ह्रीṁ devasya vāṅmana-ścakṣus...... (and so on) and then placing one’s thumb on the heart of the image. This is to be followed by the recitation of another मन्त्र oṁ asyai prāṇāḥ prati-ṣṭhantu..... (and so on) which completes the process.
In पूजा or worship also, a similar procedure is followed, at the time of every worship.

Prātiśākhya
(‘pertaining to every branch [of the वेदस्]’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस्, which are the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, are difficult to understand due to two primary reasons: the archaic language and the special phonetic system.
Out of the six Vedāṅgas—subsidiary sciences that help us to understand the Vedas—the first two, viz., the शिक्षा and the व्याकरण (phonetics and grammar) help us to unravel these two aspects.
The Prātiśākhyas are the earlier phase of development of these two aspects. Literally the word means a treatise pertaining to the particular śākhā or branch of the Veda. Going by this definition, every śākhā of the Vedas—and there were hundreds of them as mentioned in allied works—must have had its own Prāti-śākhya.
However, only very few of them—belonging to all the four Vedas—have survived till today.
They generally deal with topics like pronunciation, intonation, sandhis (rules of conjunction of letters or words), shortening or lengthening of the vowels, rules connected with the breaking up of saṁhitā-pāṭha (Vedic mantras in sentences) into पदपाठ (constituent words) and so on.
A brief description of some of these Prātiśākhyas may now be attempted here:
The Ṛkprātiśākhya of शौनक (a disciple of आश्वलायन)—also known as Śikṣāśāstra and Pārṣada—is a very ancient and important work. It is closely associated with the Saṁhitopaniṣad part of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (

). It echoes the opinions of the various ācāryas (teachers of Vedic tradition) like Māṇḍūkeya, Mākṣarya, अगस्त्य, Śūravīra and others.
It is in the form of sūtras or kaṇḍikas (short sentences in prose), with a commentary by उवट. Another commentary by Viṣṇumitra is available only for the first two sections.
There are three sections of six paṭalas (subsections) each, making a total of 18 paṭalas with 103 kaṇḍikās.
The subjects dealt with are: सṁज्ञा (definitions); sandhis or conjunctions like praśliṣṭa and udgrāha; svaras (intonations); some more sandhis like natisandhi; क्रमपाठ (a kind of breaking up of Vedic sentences); opinions of various other teachers; defects of pronunciation and intonation; traditional methods of chanting the वेदस्; about the various Vedic meters and allied subjects.
The Taittirīyaprātiśākhya has two praśnas (sections), each containing twelve adhyāyas or chapters. It is also in the form of sūtras. There are three well-known commentaries: Padakramasadana of Māhiṣeya; Tribhāṣāratna of Somayārya and Vaidikābharaṇa of Gopālayajvā.
The first of these is the most ancient one. It deals with a ‘prakṛtipāṭha’ or a basic reading of a Vedic sentence from which the पदपाठ and the क्रमपाठ can be derived. In addition it also deals with the sandhis related to the topics under consideration.
Belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda group is the Vājasaneyī Prātiśākhya of कात्यायन. He is different from the कात्यायन who has written a vārttika on पाणिनि’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, and lived earlier than Pāṇiṇi (500 B. C.).
It is also in the form of sūtras and has eight adhyāyas. The topics discussed include the characteristics of technical terms used, sandhis, rules concerning padapāṭhas, types of svaras and about the letters of the alphabet. Opinions of the ancient teachers like शाकल्य, Kāśyapa and Śākaṭāyana are mentioned. Many technical terms used by Pāṇini—such as उदात्त (level intonation), स्वरित (higher pitch intonation), āmredita (repetition) and lopa (elision)—are already found here.
Even some sūtras of this work have been repeated in the Aṣṭādhyāyī.
As regards the Sāmavedic Prāti-śakhyas two treatises are available: the Puṣpasūtra and the Ṛktantra.
The former is the composition of the sage Puṣpa. It has ten prapāṭhakas or chapters. उपाध्याय अजातशत्रु has written a bhāṣya on it. It deals mainly with the stobhas (musical interjections like ‘hā u,’ ‘hā i,’ ‘hum,’ ‘ho’, ‘ohā’ and so on, interpolated into a सामन्) giving all the details connected with them.
The Ṛktantra belongs to the Kauthumaśākhā of Sāmaveda. There are 287 sūtras in five prapāṭhakas or sections. Śākaṭāyana is its author. He precedes यास्क and Pāṇinī since the latter authors have mentioned him.
It deals mainly with the origin of the letters of the alphabet, their varieties as also some technical terms. The places of production of the letters in the mouth and sandhis have also been touched upon. For the Atharvaveda, only one treatise is available now. It is the Śaunakīyacatura-dhyāyikā. It leans more towards grammar than intonation and other details.
See also ŚIKṢĀ and VEDĀṄGAS.

pratyutthāna
(‘getting up, facing [the elders]’)
------------------------------------------
See ABHIVĀDANA.

prabhāmaṇḍala
(‘circle of light’)
------------------------------------------
Behind the icons ceremonially established in temples and meant for worship, there is, invariably, an arch of effulgence (like the solar orb). This is generally made of metal strip and encompasses the image. It is this that is called ‘prabhāmaṇḍala’ or ‘prabhāvalī’. It may be round or elliptical in shape and has ornamental designs. It is supported on either side by a pillar-like motif or structure. The top-centre part has the head of a leonine figure known as the कीर्तिमुख. (See KĪRTIMUKHA for details.)
The प्रभामण्डल is a detachable unit. The metal strip may have a support of wooden strip.
If the image in the temple is of stone, the प्रभामण्डल is also etched in stone.

pradakṣiṇa
(‘circumambulation’)
------------------------------------------
See NAMASKĀRA.

prātibha
(‘intuition’)
------------------------------------------
Many a power is hidden in the मिन्द्. Spiritual disciplines involving purification and concentration bring out these hidden powers.
One such, mentioned in the Yoga-sūtras (3.33 and 36) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) is the प्रातिभ. It is the power by which correct and clear knowledge about any object arises in the मिन्द् just by a wish, needing no other means.
It may be the knowledge concerning a very subtle object (sūkṣma), an object which is hidden (vyavahita) or at a great distance (viprakṛṣta); and also the know-ledge of past and future events.

pradhvaṁsābhāva
(‘non-existence after destruction’)
------------------------------------------
See ABHĀVA.

prastotṛ
(‘the eulogist’)
------------------------------------------
The उद्गातृ (‘chanter’), one of the four principal priests in a Vedic sacrifice, has three assistants, out of whom the प्रस्तोतृ (or prastotā) also is one. He is responsible for chanting the प्रस्ताव (the first part or prelude in a सामन् chant). He also participates in the prasarpaṇa (ritual procession of priests to the āstāva, a place meant for chanting). It is again he who sings solo, a laudatory hymn to यम (the god of death) after the horse is immolated in the अश्वमेध sacrifice.
See also UDGĀTṚ.

prāṇaliṅga
------------------------------------------
See under VĪRAŚAIVISM included in ŚAIVISM.

pratihāra
------------------------------------------
The उद्गातृ is one of the four principal priests in a Vedic sacrifice, representing the Sāmaveda and singing the sāmans at the appropriate stages in a sacrifice. He has three assistants one of whom is the pratihartṛ or pratihartā. It is his duty to chant the प्रतिहार (a part of the सामन्, introduced with the chant huṁ). The प्रतिहार is like a reply or response to प्रस्ताव, the first part of a सामन्.
See also SĀMAN.

prācīnāvīta
[(the sacred thread) that is worn after taking it round’]
------------------------------------------
According to the धर्मशास्त्रस् (secondary scriptures dealing with the वर्ण-आश्रम-dharmas and related topics) every ‘dvija’ (‘the twice-born’) must wear the यज्ञोपवीत or the उपवीत (the sacred thread). This is normally worn on the left shoulder, its right part hanging below the right arm. This mode of wearing, called the यज्ञोपवीत-mode, is maintained for all normal religious rites concerning the gods or the deities. However, in the rites concerning the पितृस् or manes (for e.g., śrāddha ceremonies) this mode of wearing is reversed. The thread is worn on right shoulder, the lower part hanging below the left arm. This is called ‘prācīnāvīta’ mode or ‘āvīta’ mode.
See also YAJÑOPAVĪTA.

prātas-savana
(‘morning extraction [of the सोम juice]’)
------------------------------------------
See SAVANA.

pratiṣṭhāpana
(‘establishing’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in the consecration of a new temple, chiefly in the sense of infusing the divine presence in the image through appropriate rituals and āvāhanamantras (incantations of invitation and welcome).
See TEMPLES (HINDU) for details.

Pravargya
------------------------------------------
It is a Vedic sacrificial rite. Though considered as an independent rite, it is actually incorporated in the Somayāgas like the अग्निष्टोम. It is generally performed twice a day for three days.
An important item of this sacrifice is the preparation of gharma (hot milk mixed with boiling ghee) out of the milk of a cow and a she-goat, along with ghee.
The offerings of gharma are made through fire to the deities अश्विन्स्, वायु, इन्द्र, Savitṛ, बृहस्पति and यम.
The sacrificer drinks the remainder from the upayamanī (the supporting ladle used in the oblations).
During the performance of the प्रवर्ग्य rite, the doors of the prācīna-vaṁśa or the sacrificial shed are kept closed.

pratiṣedha
(‘prohibition’)
------------------------------------------
It is the same as ‘niṣedha’ used in the पूर्वमीमाṁसा works. See NIṢEDHA for details.
In Sanskrit literature, the word is used to indicate a kind of अलङ्कार (figure of speech) wherein the sentence gives a meaning entirely different from its direct sense.

pratyagātman
(‘the Self inside’)
------------------------------------------
This word actually refers to the आत्मन् or the Self within our heart (vide Kaṭha Upaniṣad 4.1). It is interpreted either as परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self) or as the jīvātman (the individual सोउल्).
See also ĀTMAN.

Prahlāda
------------------------------------------
Prahlāda, the king of child-devotees of Lord विष्णु, was the eldest son of Hiraṇyākaśipu, the powerful king of the दैत्यस् or demons. His मोथेर् was Kayādhu, the daughter of the demon-king Jambhāsura. She too, being initiated by the great sage नारद, was a devotee of विष्णु.
His story is delineated in detail in the Bhāgavata (7.4 to 8) and the Viṣṇupurāṇa (1.17).
He alienated his ड़थेर्, who was an inveterate hater of Lord विष्णु, by his matchless devotion to विष्णु. All the efforts of हिरण्यकशिपु to get him killed were set at naught by the protection विष्णु gave him. Ultimately विष्णु killed Hiraṇya-kaśipu by assuming the नरसिṁह (Man-lion) form. प्रह्लाद’s prayer to the Lord नरसिṁह liberated हिरण्यकशिपु from all his sins.
Prahlāda’s teaching about the navavidhabhakti or the nine modes of devotion (vide Bhāgavata 7.5.23) is widely accepted and acclaimed.
He had four brothers and three sons as also a daughter.
The famous king बलि who too was a great devotee of विष्णु, was his grandson.
Prahlāda has been shown in the पुराणस् as having had many learned discussions with others like बलि, हṁस, इन्द्र and the sage Ajagara, about धर्म.

pramā
(‘the knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu philosophical treatises often use four technical terms: प्रमा, pramāṇa, prameya and pramātṛ.
An object that has to be known is ‘prameya’. The means of knowledge that gives us its correct understanding is ‘pramāṇa’. The correct knowledge that is got through the प्रमाणस् is ‘pramā’.
For instance, a pot is ‘prameya’. The eye that sees it and the process of seeing is ‘pramāṇa’. The knowledge got that it is a mud pot of small size, black in colour, containing water, is ‘pramā’.
The person who knows it thus is the pramātṛ (knower).
Pramā is true knowledge which is not negated by later perceptions. If negated—like seeing a snake in a rope in insufficient light and then discovering it in bright light that it is a rope—it is only a भ्रम (illusion or false perception).
Sometimes, false knowledge is called apramā and three more varieties of it are predicated: स्मृति (insufficient memory), सṁशय (doubt) and तर्क (false लोगिच्).
See also PRAMĀṆAS.

Prabhāsa
(‘[a place that] shines brilliantly’)
------------------------------------------
Prabhāsa—also known as प्रभास Paṭṭaṇa—is an ancient and famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे containing the renowned सोम्नाथ् तेम्प्ले. (See SOMANĀTHA TEMPLE for its details.) It is situated in the Kathewar region of Gujarat State in western India.
During the days of the Mahābhārata it was a well-known and flourishing city. The Pāṇḍavas had visited this place of पिल्ग्रिमगे since it was at the confluence of the three holy rivers Hiraṇyā, Kapilā and सरस्वती which joined the sea here. It was here that अर्जुन, the famous Pāṇḍava hero, abducted सुभद्रा (sister of Śrī कृष्ण) with his help. Again, it was here that the Yādava race exterminated itself by infighting after which बलराम and Śrī कृष्ण gave up their bodies.
There ia a small temple, built in the recent years—maybe on the ruins of an old one—at the spot where Śrī कृष्ण is said to have given up his physical body.
There are a few other temples here dedicated to महाकाल (Śiva), गणेश and बलराम.
Purāṇas like the Skānda extol its greatness in hyperbolic terms. For instance: It was here that चन्द्र (Moon-god) was cured of his disease of consumption. The alligators in the sea here are harmless. The लिङ्ग (in the सोम्नाथ् तेम्प्ले) is one of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस्, and so on.

Pravāhaṇa Jaivali
------------------------------------------
Pravāhaṇa, the son of Jaivala—hence called Pravāhaṇa Jaivali—was the king of Pāñcāla. He was once holding a big meeting of scholars. श्वेतकेतु, the son of गौतम आरुणि, arrived there with a view to taking part in the philosophical disputations and earn some wealth and fame. However, he was unable to answer even one of the five questions put to him by the king. Feeling disgraced, he returned home and took his ड़थेर् to task for not having taught this science that could have helped him to answer these questions. Since गौतम too did not know it, he went in all humility to the king प्रवाहण जैवलि and learnt it from him.
This story appears in both the Chāndogya (5.3) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2) उपनिषद्स्.
In the first chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (1.8.1-8) also there appears one प्रवाहण जैवलि, one of the three who had assembled to discuss about the उद्गीथ (a part of सामन् or Sāmaveda मन्त्र). He proves his superiority over the others.
In the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (1.38.4) also there is the mention of one Jaivali. He too could be the same person.

prāyaścitta
(‘expiation’)
------------------------------------------
Sin and its expiation is one of the important subjects discussed by the Hindu scriptures, especially the धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस्.
The general name for an expiation is ‘prāyaścitta’. It is defined in various ways:
A firm resolve (citta) to undergo तपस् or austerity (prāya).
Purification (citta) from the effects of sins (= prāya).
Destruction (= prāya) of sins and regaining the original pure state (citta).
For details, see PĀTAKA.

Prakāśānanda Yati
------------------------------------------
Prakāśānanda यति, a disciple of Jñānānanda यति, is one of the well-known writers of Advaita Vedānta in the post-शङ्कर (A.

-820) period. He might have lived during the last part of the 15th and the first part of the 16th centuries. His most famous work is the Vedāntasiddhānta-muktāvalī.
He is the primary propounder of the two doctrines ‘dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda’ and the ‘ekajīvavāda’.
See ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.

Prākṛt
(‘unrefined’)
------------------------------------------
Sanskrit (or सṁस्कृत) and प्राकृत् (or Prākṛta) are two important languages of ancient India.
‘Prākṛta’ as against ‘saṁskṛta’ means, ‘the unrefined, the original or the basic’. Taken in this sense, it is the crude form of Sanskrit, the crudeness being brought about by corruption in usage by the common masses.
If Sanskrit was the language of the classes, प्राकृत् was the language of the masses.
Considered as a vernacular dialect, प्राकृत् could have existed in many forms. The names of these were: Apabhraṁśa, Mahārāṣṭrī, Māgadhī, Paiśācī and Śaurasenī.
The Jain scriptures like the Ācārāṅga and the Sūtrakṛtāṅga as also the edicts of अशोक (272-232 B. C.) and Khāravela (200 B. C.) are in प्राकृत्.
There are a large number of works including grammars and dictionaries in this language. The subjects covered are poetics, अस्त्रोलोग्य् and medical sciences, apart from religion.

prasthānatraya
(‘the three basic treatises [of Vedānta]’)
------------------------------------------
Among the six systems of Hindu philosophy—generally called the Ṣaḍ-darśanas—the Vedānta system is certainly the crest-jewel. With a balanced combination of great respect for the वेदस् and incontrovertible लोगिच् that demolishes the non-Vedic systems, it has earned for itself an unenviable place among the well-known philosophies of the world.
The Vedānta system is built primarily on the प्रस्थानत्रय, the three foundational works that take one to the final goal of life (= prasthāna). They are: the Śrutiprasthāna (Upaniṣads); the स्मृति-prasthāna (the Bhagavadgītā) and the Nyāyaprasthāna (the Brahmasūtras).
Of these three, the उपनिषद्स् being the Śruti, the cardinal scripture of Hindu-ism, are of utmost importance.
The Brahmasūtras, being a systematisation of the philosophy of the उपनिषद्स्, helps in building up the metaphysical frame of Vedānta.
The Bhagavadgītā, being an extremely popular and highly venerated work, had to be admitted into the prasthāna group.

prātaranuvāka
(‘morning litany’)
------------------------------------------
In the Somayāgas—sacrifices requiring the oblation of the सोम juice—the day on which the juice is extracted is called the ‘sutyā’. On the previous night, during its last part, the होतृ priest recites several mantras, technically called ‘prāta-ranuvāka’. It is generally chanted by him sitting between the two हविर्धान carts (carrying the vessels full of the सोम plants or stalks).
The litany comprises three sections. The total number of ṛks (Ṛgvedic mantras) to be chanted varies from 100 to 360, and, sometimes up to 1000!
The pitch of the voice while chanting them has to be gradually raised through seven tones.

Prakāśātman
(A.

-820). The work deals with only the first four sūtras of the Brahmasūtras, शङ्कर’s bhāśya on it and पद्मपाद’s gloss on शङ्कर’s bhāṣya.
This famous work has given rise to a new school of Advaita, known as the ‘Vivaraṇaprasthāna’.
See also ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.
