Pratardana
------------------------------------------
Pratardana, the king of काशी, was the son of दिवोदास and Mādhavī. His story appears first in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇopaniṣad (

) of the Ṛgveda.
By the dint of his prowess and heroism, he goes to the world of इन्द्र who asks him to choose any boon. Though प्रतर्दन refuses to ask any, Indra—identified here with Supreme Brahman—teaches him about his own greatness and asks him to meditate on himself (i. e., इन्द्र) as प्राण (life-force) and prajñātman (the Intelligent Self).
The entire section is known as Pratardanavidyā or Prāṇavidyā.
The story as given in the Mahā-bhārata (Anuśāsanaparva 30) states that the king प्रतर्दन whose race had almost been exterminated by the हैहय king वीतहव्य and his sons, went in pursuit of the fleeing वीतहव्य. The latter was given shelter by the sage भृगु who protected him. Hence प्रतर्दन had to return to his kingdom without destroying his enemy.
However, by the grace of the sage भृगु, वीतहव्य became a ब्राह्मण of highly sāttvik nature; and, प्रतर्दन gave up his enmity.
See also KAUṢĪTAKI ब्राह्मण UPANIṢAD.

pratyavarohaṇa
(‘re-descent’)
------------------------------------------
India possesses more varieties of serpents than any single country in the world.
Serpent-worship, which is common even today, must have arisen from the fear entertained about the deadly effects of snakebites. Hence, the serpent-cult (nāgapūjā and nāgabali) here may be considered as very ancient.
The dangers posed by snakes get intensified during the rainy season since their places of dwelling get drowned under water.
To ward off the dangers, the rite of offering a बलि (oblation or a sacrifice) to serpents was performed on the Śrāvaṇa-pūrṇimā day (full-मोओन् day in the month of Śrāvaṇa, generally in August) and continued everyday for four months till Mārgaśīrṣa-pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, generally in December).
Till this day, people were using (or advised to use) cots or some high furniture (inaccessible to snakes) which they were expected to discard now, get down (= प्रत्यवरोहण) and sleep on the ground!
Thus प्रत्यवरोहण became a reli-gious rite.

pratibandhikalpanā
(‘showing the same defect in the opposite party’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the eleven modes of तर्क or लोगिच्.
The न्याय philosophy states that the paramāṇus (atoms) are without parts, but can combine to produce bigger material objects. If the Vedāntin raises the objection that a partless परमाणु can never come into contact with another परमाणु which is also partless, the न्याय-philosopher raises a similar objection regarding ब्रह्मन् which is all-pervading (and hence without parts), viz., how it can come into contact with the objects of this world like pots. This type of raising a counter objection is called प्रतिबन्धिकल्पना.

Prapañcasāra
------------------------------------------
INTRODUCTION
The तन्त्रस् are a special class of literature dealing mainly with the upāsanā aspect—meditation and rituals—of हिन्दुइस्म्. (See TANTRAS for details.)
One of the earliest and pre-eminent of these तन्त्रस् is the Prapañcasāra or Prapañcasāratantra, attributed to Ādi शङ्कर (A.

-820). On this work there is a well-known commentary called Vivaraṇa by पद्मपाद, one of the four chief disciples of शङ्कर and the first pontiff of the Kālikāmaṭha at द्वारका (in Gujarat).
Whether this work dealing with mantras, yantras and upāsanā of the various deities of the Hindu pantheon is a genuine composition of the famous शङ्कर, or someone else’s passed on as his, there is no doubt that it is the handiwork of a great genius.
The work has 2470 verses distributed among 36 paṭalas or chapters dealing with various topics such as च्रेअतिओन् and dissolution, development of the human embryo and birth, letters of the alphabet, bījākṣaras or seed-letters, दीक्षा or initiation as also the mantras and rituals connected with the various deities.
A brief summary of this treatise may now be attempted here:
Chapter 1 (104 verses)
It starts with the questions of ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and रुद्र put to Lord नारायण.
Nārāyaṇa replies that they were brought forth by अक्षर (the Eternal-Imperishable or ब्रह्मन्). He then proceeds to describe the process of च्रेअतिओन् beginning with पुरुष (soul) and प्रकृति (matter).
A detailed description of the concept of time starting with लव (a split-second) right up to the life of the four-faced ब्रह्मा (which is equal to 17,280 million human years) has also been given here.
Chapter 2 (67 verses)
Development of the embryo within the मोथेर्’s womb and certain other topics of आयुर्वेद are dealt with in this chapter.
Another subject discussed here is that of bhāvas or sounds and several aspects of कुण्डलिनी.
Chapter 3 (75 verses)
The main theme of this chapter is the letters of the alphabet classified as saumya (lunar), saura (solar) and āgneya (fiery).
How these letters are uttered by the working of the air, first through the सुषुम्ना canal and then through the vocal organ is also described.
Incidentally, the names of 50 oṣadhis (herbs) like चन्दन (sandal), aguru (fragrant aloe) and karpūra (camphor) have also been mentioned here.
Chapter 4 (76 verses)
This chapter deals mainly with the बीजाक्षर (seed-letter) hrīm, variously called ‘nāda,’ ‘prāṇa’, ‘jīva,’ ‘ghoṣa’ and so on.
It is identified with the devatā (goddess) भुवनेश्वरी, also known as Kuṇḍalī.
The Haṁsamantra (so’haṁ haṁ saḥ) too, also called ‘Mahāvākya’, finds a mention here.
Chapter 5 (70 verses)
Henceforward, this work deals mostly with rituals, normal to such tāntrik works.
The topics dealt with here, are: दीक्षा (initiation), मन्त्र (sacred formula), vāstumaṇḍala and vāstudevatā as also vāstubali (rites connected with the वास्तुपुरुष, a cosmic deity), and erection of a मण्डप (a small structure, a shed) for purposes of दीक्षा.
Chapter 6 (125 verses)
The topics included in this chapter are: the ṛṣi (sage), छन्दस् (metre) and devatā (deity) of a मन्त्र; nyāsas (six or five); worship of the deity; establishing of the kumbha (pot); प्राणप्रतिष्ठा (infusing life into the image or symbol); the उपचारस् (special modes of offering); होम (fire-sacrifice); offering unto ब्रह्मन्; praṇāma (obeisance).
Chapter 7 (70 verses)
This chapter deals with the rules of sādhana concerning सरस्वती, the goddess of speech.
For her मन्त्र, ब्रह्मा is the ṛṣi, गायत्री is the छन्दस् (metre) and सरस्वती herself is the devatā (deity).
The dhyānaśloka describes her form for meditation as having three eyes and of transparent brilliance. She is white in colour and holds a rosary, a pot of nectar and a book in three hands, the fourth showing the cintāmudrā (the pose of knowledge or wisdom).
Her nine attendants include the goddesses Medhā (understanding), Prabhā (radiance) and स्मृति (memory).
Other details concerning जप and होम are also given.
Chapter 8 (60 verses)
The first part of this chapter deals with prāṇāgni-होम. In the mūlādhāracakra (where the कुण्डलिनी is resting) five homakuṇḍas (pits for sacrificial fires) are imagined to exist and offerings of the letters of the alphabet are to be poured into them.
The second part deals with the worship of सरस्वती which includes the steps like न्यास (ritual purification of limbs), पूजा (worship) as also a beautiful hymn on her.
Chapter 9 (44 verses)
This chapter is devoted to the worship of the goddess Tripurā. She is called ‘Tripurā’ since she is the creatrix of the trimūrtis—Brahmā, विष्णु and महेश्वर. She is also the three वेदस् and existed even before च्रेअतिओन्, filling all the space. Her bījas (seed-letters) are aim and klīm.
Other items dealt with are the dhyānaśloka (hymn of meditation), and her attendant goddesses like Vāmā and a चक्र (diagram). The effects of worshipping her are also described.
Chapter 10 (69 verses)
Worship of Mūlaprakṛti (known as भुवनेश्वरी or Bhuvaneśī also) along with her मन्त्र, होम, अभिषेक (ritual bath) and जप as also other allied subjects are discussed here.
The dhyānaśloka describes her form with पाश (noose), aṅkuśa (goad) in two hands and exhibiting the abhaya and varada (offering protection and boon-giving) mudrās in the other two hands.
Chapter 11 (70 verses)
The same topic is continued here with some additional information about her यन्त्र, Gāyatrīmantra and attendant goddesses. There is also a long hymn addressed to her, towards the end.
Chapter 12 (65 verses)
In this chapter, a detailed exposition of the worship of Śrī or लक्ष्मी is given. For her मन्त्र, भृगु is the ṛṣi (sage), nivṛt is the छन्दस् (metre) and Śrī or लक्ष्मी is the devatā or deity.
The dhyānaśloka describes her as holding two lotuses in her two upper hands whereas the two lower hands exhibit the abhaya and the varada mudrās. Two elephants are also pouring घृत (ghee or clarified butter) from two pots.
After describing जप (repetition of her divine name) and होम (fire-worship), the text gives how her nine Śaktis are to be invoked round her पीठ (seat).
She is also described as Ramā, and 32 Śaktis (or aspects) like भारती, पार्वती, Cāndrī are enumerated.
Her worship leads to the attainment of purity, bodily perfection, beauty and intelligence.
Chapter 13 (90 verses)
Dealing with the goddess Tripuṭā, this section gives the ṛṣi, छन्दस् and devatā as Varāha, nivṛt and Dharaṇī.
The जप of her मन्त्र has to be done twelve lakh times.
The other topics discussed are the मन्त्र of the goddess Tvaritā, yantras with ten and twelve lines, मन्त्र of the deity Nityā and associated rites.
Chapter 14 (88 verses)
This chapter deals exclusively with the goddess दुर्गा including her several aspects and Śaktis (attendant deities).
Aspects of दुर्गा are वनदुर्गा and Śūlinīdurgā.
Mantras of all these aspects and their methods of पुरश्चरण (ceremonial repetition) are also given.
It is specially mentioned here that supplication to दुर्गा as Vindhyavāsinī can eradicate the effects of all kinds of poisons like those of snakes, scorpions, rats and dogs.
Chapter 15 (65 verses)
This chapter concerns सूर्य or the Sun-god and his four-lettered मन्त्र.
Aja (Brahmā) is the ṛṣi for this मन्त्र whereas गायत्री is the छन्दस्. Bhuvaneśī—an aspect of the Divine Mother—is the devatā.
As in other cases, here also the dhyānaśloka (for meditation), nyāsas, होम and other rituals have been described.
Chapter 16 (65 verses)
This chapter deals with the मन्त्र of चन्द्र or सोम (the मोओन्), his worship and his nine Śaktis like रोहिणी, कृत्तिका, Revatī and भरणी.
It also gives the मन्त्र of अग्नि and his nine Śaktis such as Pītā, Śvetā, Dhūmrā, Rucirā and Jvālinī.
Chapter 17 (78 verses)
This section deals with Mahā-गणपति.
The मन्त्र is a long one with 28 letters. Its ṛṣi is Gaṇaka, the छन्दस् is nivṛt and the deity is Mahāgaṇapati.
The dhyānaśloka describes him along with his शक्ति (who is wearing shining ornaments and holding a lotus in her hand). He has ten arms holding pomegranate fruit, mace, discus, noose, his own tusk and so on.
He has nine Śaktis like Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Ugrā, Kāmarūpiṇī and others.
Other mantras including a गणेश-गायत्री are also given.
Chapter 18 (54 verses)
This is devoted to मन्मथ (Cupid), the god of love. For his मन्त्र, Sammohana is the ṛṣi, गायत्री is the छन्दस् and Manobhāva is the deity. He has eight Śaktis to assist him, like Mohanī, Trāsī, Ākarṣiṇī and so on.
Two mantras are given. The first is of a single letter. The second, called mālāmantra, has fifty letters.
A मन्त्र of Ratividyā (Kāma’s consort) consisting of 32 letters is also indicated.
This section gives a long मन्त्र of श्रीकृष्ण (of 18 letters) and the ways of using it.
Chapter 19 (64 verses)
The subjects dealt with in this chapter are: प्रणव (Oṅkāra), meditation on विष्णु, the four व्यूहस् of विष्णु, details concerning योग like यम and नियम, five states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, different states of योग and the yogasiddhis like अणिमा (capacity to become small like an atom) and so on.
Methods of utkrānti (leaving the body through its various parts), entering into others’ bodies and returning are also described towards the end.
Chapter 20 (61 verses)
The aṣṭākṣarīmantra—the famous eight-lettered मन्त्र of Nārāyaṇa—is the main subject here. Of this मन्त्र, Sādhyanārāyaṇa is the ṛṣi, गायत्री is the छन्दस् and परमात्मन् is the devatā.
Apart from giving the names of the ten avatāras—which list omits बुद्ध but includes Balarāma—some aspects of rituals like arcana (worship) and जप (repetition of the divine मन्त्र) are also dealt with at the end.
Chapter 21 (60 verses)
This chapter deals with the twelve yantras or diagrams of the twelve rāśis or signs of the zodiac. Bhānu (or the Sun) when associated with these twelve rāśis has twelve different names such as Dhātā, Aryamā, मित्र, Vivasvān, Pūṣā and so on.
Towards the end, a beautiful hymn addressed to विष्णु is also given.
Chapter 22 (58 verses)
The dvādaśākṣarī (twelve-lettered) मन्त्र of Lord वासुदेव is the subject of this section. प्रजापति is the ṛṣi whereas गायत्री is the छन्दस्. विष्णु is the devatā.
It is to be repeated twelve lakh times and is capable of giving मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Three kinds of nyāsas—saṁhāra-न्यास, sṛṣṭinyāsa and sthitinyāsa—leading to the destruction of doṣas (faults), and the च्रेअतिओन् of good, as also gaining peace are also given.
Incidentally, the मन्त्र of सुदर्शन (Lord विष्णु’s discus) and some associated rituals are also given.
Chapter 23 (72 verses)
This chapter deals with the पुरुषोत्तम aspect of Lord विष्णु. The names of his twelve aspects—like Satyātman, Acyutātman and Apratirūpa—associated with twelve parts of the body for their ceremonial purification are also given.
The ṛṣi, छन्दस् and devatā are respectively, जैमिनि, जगती and पुरुषोत्तम.
Other mantras mentioned are those of the सुदर्शनचक्र (discus), पाञ्चजन्य-शङ्ख (conch), Kaumodakīgadā (mace), गरुड (the eagle-mount) and so on.
The gāyatrīmantra of विष्णु as Trailokyamohana (one who enchants all the three worlds) as also the description of his extremely bewitching form are given towards the end.
Chapter 24 (48 verses)
The mantras, meditation and worship of Śrīkara (Lord विष्णु who produces wealth) and Mahāvarāha (the Great-boar इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) are the subject matter of this section.
Chapter 25 (58 verses)
Meditation and worship of Nṛsiṁha (man-lion इन्चर्नतिओन् of Lord विष्णु) are the main topics here.
The मन्त्र is in the anuṣṭubh metre.
Nārada or प्रजापति is said to be its ṛṣi whereas anuṣṭubh is the छन्दस्; and, the devatā is Nṛsiṁha.
He can be worshipped in two aspects: prasanna (benign) and krūra (fearsome).
Garuḍamantra and Nṛsiṁhayantra (mystic diagram) are the other topics dealt with.
Chapter 26 (66 verses)
It deals with Viṣṇupañjarayantra, a mystical diagram that affords protection to the devotee. A मन्त्र of sixteen letters (of वासुदेव), other mantras related to the weapons like the सुदर्शनचक्र (the discus) and Śārṅgadhanus (the bow) are also given.
A मन्त्र that integrates the śloka of the Gītā (11.36) describing the lord’s विश्वरूप (Cosmic Form) is also given with all the allied instructions.
Chapter 27 (73 verses)
This chapter is concerned with the prāsāda मन्त्र, a मन्त्र of Lord शिव that helps the sādhaka to get what he wants by pleasing the Lord.
Vāmadeva is the ṛṣi of this मन्त्र. The छन्दस् is paṅkti. Īśa (Śiva) is the devatā.
The dhyānaśloka describes him as pañcavaktra, having five faces. These five faces or aspects are: सद्योजात, वामदेव, अघोर, Tatpuruṣa and ईशान.
There is also an exquisite hymn on शिव (verses 55 to 64).
Chapter 28 (55 verses)
Dakṣiṇāmūrti, an important aspect of शिव, is the subject matter of this chapter. He is described as sitting under a vaṭavṛkṣa (banyan tree), white in complexion, with matted hair ornamented by the crescent मोओन्. He has four hands, holding the परशु (battle-axe) and the mṛga (deer) in two hands. The third is showing the ज्ञानमुद्रा (posture of giving spiritual wisdom) and the last rests on his knee.
For his mantra—a long one of eighteen letters—Śuka is the ṛṣi, anuṣṭubh is the छन्दस् and दक्षिणामूर्ति-रुद्र is the devatā.
The rest of the chapter deals with the connected rituals.
Chapter 29 (46 verses)
Umeśa and Ardhanārīśvara are the two aspects of Lord शिव dealt with here.
These descriptions are given in the respective dhyānaślokas. So also the rules for their जप and होम.
Ardhanārīśvara can be propitiated for various purposes such as puṣṭikarma (nourishment), śāntikarma (offsetting the evil effects of inauspicious प्लनेत्स् etc.) and even ākarṣaṇa (attracting others) as also vaśīkaraṇa (gaining control over others).
The मन्त्र of चण्डेश्वर, a fierce aspect of Lord शिव is also given, along with his गायत्री.
Chapter 30 (73 verses)
The special subject of this chapter is the famous Gāyatrīmantra, along with the प्रणव (Om), the three व्याहृतिस्, the seven व्याहृतिस् and the गायत्री-śiras.
The three vyāhṛis are: bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ and svaḥ or suvaḥ.
The seven व्याहृतिस् are: bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ, mahaḥ, janaḥ, tapaḥ and satyam.
The gāyatrīśiras is: om āpo jyotī raso’mṛtam bhūrbhuvassuvarom.
A detailed meaning and significance of all these is also described.
Chapter 31 (103 verses)
This section gives the triṣṭubh-मन्त्र of the goddess कात्यायनी (an aspect of पार्वती or दुर्गा). Actually it comprises the first four lines of the Durgā-sūkta which is a part of the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (

).
Marīcī-Kāśyapa is the ṛṣi of this मन्त्र. Triṣṭubh (a Vedic metre of 11 letters in each of the four lines) is the metre whereas Jātavedas-अग्नि is the devatā.
Apart from the ध्यान of the goddess कात्यायनी, this section also gives the names of her nine Śaktis like Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrakālī and दुर्गा.
As a part of the पूजा (worship) of the deity, names of some more goddesses like Jāgatā, Vedagarbhā, Tapanī and Dahanarūpiṇī, associated with the letters of the मन्त्र, are also given.
An interesting point made out here is that the repetition of the मन्त्र (jātavedase sunavāma and so on) in the reverse order makes it an astra or weapon capable of destroying all the defects in the ritualistic process undertaken.
Divisions of the nakṣatras into three groups (daiva, āsura and mānuṣa) and certain magical rites like stambhana (arresting), vaśīkaraṇa (subjugating others), ākarṣaṇa (attracting someone to oneself) and so on, are the other topics dealt with.
Chapter 32 (64 verses)
This section deals with the Lavaṇa-मन्त्र, related to the goddesses रात्रि, दुर्गा and Bhadrakālī. Aṅgīrā is the ṛṣi and the metres are anuṣṭubh as also triṣṭubh.
The dhyānaśloka of the कात्यायनी form of दुर्गा describes her with three eyes and four arms holding चक्र (discus), शङ्ख (conch), asi (sword) and śūla (spear).
Some magical rites like māraṇa (killing enemies) and vaśīkaraṇa (controlling a person whom we want) are also described.
Chapter 33 (72 verses)
The anuṣṭubh मन्त्र of 32 letters is dealt with here. वसिष्ठ is the ṛṣi, रुद्र is the devatā and anuṣṭubh itself is the छन्दस्.
A detailed description of रुद्र is given by the dhyānaśloka. His 32 Śaktis such as Ramā, राका, Sārā, Umā, Śāntā and Amoghā are mentioned too.
There is also the mention of a मन्त्र of 100 letters (śatākṣaramantra), formed by combining the letters of the three metres—gāyatrī, triṣṭubh and anuṣṭubh. Its repetition gives longevity.
Chapter 34 (77 verses)
This chapter deals with a number of rites that can bring about the following results: longevity; cure of fever; controlling the minds of others; attracting others to oneself; conquering of enemies and so on.
Chapter 35 (22 verses)
Prāṇapratiṣṭhā or infusing life into an image or a यन्त्र (geometrical diagram of a deity) is the subject matter here. प्राण or life force is considered as a deity and her description is given in a ध्यान-śloka. She has three eyes. She is seated on a lotus situated in a boat. She is holding in her hands पाश (noose), ikṣu-kodaṇḍa and pañcabāṇas (bow of sugarcane, with five arrows) as also aṅkuśa (goad) and asṛk-कपाल (skull-cup with blood).
Her companions are Mṛtā, Vaivasvatā, Prāṇalā, Ākṛṣyā and others.
Chapter 36 (63 verses)
This concluding chapter starts with the condemnation of a person who does not have a son or sons, the reasons for the same and the remedies like the performance of a यज्ञ (sacrifice).
It also describes the qualifications of a गुरु (spiritual preceptor, especially the one who gives a मन्त्र and gets all the rituals performed) such as competence in this science, capacity to bless or chastise, conquest of the six enemies (like lust), deep knowledge of the scriptures, being devoted to the worship of God, infinite patience, compassion towards the disciples, capacity of good speech in order to teach well and so on.
The disciple too must deserve his grace by cultivating the following virtues: humility, devotion to the गुरु as if he is God Himself, service to him, observing truth and celibacy strictly, being controlled in eating, sleep and speech, deep interest in studies, eschewing calumny and so on.
Why this work is called Prapañcasāra is explained at the end. It is the sāra (essence) of the prapañca (the world).
The treatise ends with a prayer of God as ‘paripūrṇatejas’ (Overfull or Perfect Light).
Conclusion
The Prapañcasāra is a difficult work to understand since it contains an esoteric spiritual science. Such sciences used to be taught privately in the seclusion of forest monasteries or academies. That is why they were either in the form of sūtras (aphorisms) or couched in an apparently unintelligible language. Only those who could unearth their special terms or symbols, could understand them.
Though the commentary Vivaraṇa of पद्मपाद does throw light on the many aspects of this work, it still leaves much unsaid or unexplained, especially in the field of the various mantras. Since the tradition that these mantras were to be transmitted directly and secretly by the गुरु to the disciple was till very strong (and inviolable) during his time, पद्म-pāda must have played it safe by strictly following it.
However, the work Prapañcasāra-sārasaṅgraha of Gīrvāṇendra सरस्वती has untied the knots in many places and has made it easier to understand and follow.

prāṇamayakośa
(‘the sheath of प्राण or life’)
------------------------------------------
It is the पञ्चप्राणस् or the five vital airs, along with the कर्मेन्द्रियस् or organs of action, that constitute the प्राणमयकोश. They cover the सोउल् like a sheath, hiding its real nature, which is चैतन्य or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.

pratyabhivāda
(‘returning the salutation’)
------------------------------------------
If अभिवादन or bowing down to elders and superiors is obligatory for the youngsters and inferiors, it is equally obligatory for the latter to respond to it appropriately. This response is called प्रत्यभिवाद.
This generally takes the form of a blessing like ‘āyuṣmān bhava’ (‘May you live long!’), ‘saubhāgyavatī bhava’ ([To a woman] ‘May you remain dear to your husband!’). The name of the person is also added at the end and the last vowel is lengthened to pluta (three mātras). For instance: ‘āyuṣmān bhava devadattā3.’
It is interesting to note that social hierarchies are meticulously kept up in this act, the way of response being dependent upon the social status of the respondent vis-a-vis the person who bows down first.

prātibhāsika
(‘an apparent [reality]’)
------------------------------------------
See PĀRAMĀRTHIKA.

Prayogamañjarī
------------------------------------------
The Prayogamañjarī or the Mañjarī for short, is one of the earliest and the most important compendiums dealing with temple construction and temple rituals. Later works like Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati and Tantrasamuccaya have drawn upon this work quoting profusely from it.
Though it is concerned more with the temples of Kerala, there is enough material for those who want to study about हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् and the associated rituals.
The author of this work is Ravi, a Nampūtiri (or नम्बूदिरि) ब्राह्मण scholar. He is believed to have lived between the 10th and 11th centuries A. D. His ड़थेर् was Aṣṭamūrti and he belonged to the Kāśyapagotra. The family belonged to the lineage known as Māṭharakula. His place has been identified with the modern Cemparakulangara shrine area in Northern Kerala.
The work has a Sanskrit commentary by त्रिविक्रम (15th century A. D.).
The Prayogamañjarī has 21 paṭalas or chapters. They are:
Ācāryaparigraha (selection of the preceptor); Bhūparigraha (taking possession of the site for building the temple); Vāstuyāga (ceremonies to purify the site) Iṣṭakādhāna (laying of the bricks for the basement); गर्भाधान (construction of the sanctum sanctorum wherein the image of the deity is to be installed for worship); Prāsādalakṣaṇa (styles and types of temples); Śilālakṣaṇa (varieties of the stone granite); Liṅgalakṣaṇa (specifications of the idol); दीक्षा (vows of the preceptor); Aṅkura (sowing of the seeds to test the fertility of the land); Jalādhivāsana (placing the idol in holy water); Rākṣoghna-vāstu (rites for destroying the evil effects); Liṅgaśuddhi (purification of the idol with different materials); Adhivāsana (preliminary purification before the installation); Pratiṣṭhā (the ceremony of installation); Arcanā (ritualistic worship); Caturthadivasa snapana (bathing the idol on the fourth day); उत्सव (festivals); Tīrtha-snānavidhi (dipping of the idol in holy ghāṭs); स्नान (ceremonial bath) Jīrṇoddhāravidhi (rules for the renovation of dilapidated shrines).
The treatment is general and therefore can be adopted in the case of any deity, with minor variations where needed.

prājāpatya
(‘related to प्रजापति’)
------------------------------------------
Listed among the kṛcchras (a kind of expiations for sins), the प्राजापत्य is spread over four periods of three days each. The person observing it has to eat once only by day during the first period, once only by night during the second period, eat only that ड़ोओद् which may be got unasked during the third period and fast completely on the last three days.
This order may also be reversed.
While prescribing a कृच्छ्र, if no particular name—such as तप्तकृच्छ्र or parṇakṛcchra—is mentioned, then it is to be understood that it is the प्राजापत्य that is referred to.
The word also means the ब्राह्मी-मुहूर्त (45 minutes before sunrise) and a form of मर्रिअगे (one of the eight varieties). See VIVĀHA for details.
See also KṚCCHRA.

Prabhākara
(8th cent. A. D.)
------------------------------------------
The Mīmāṁsā philosophy, one of the six systems of Hindu philosophy, is based primarily on the Pūrvamīmāṁsāsūtras of जैमिनि (400 B. C.). Out of the several bhāṣyas (commentaries) known to have existed on that basic work, only that of शबरस्वामिन् (A.

) has survived to this day.
Prabhākara भट्ट (or प्रभाकर) and Kumārila were the two most important teachers of this school who have written commentaries on the Bhāṣya of Śabara. They were contemporaries.
Prabhākara—nicknamed as ‘Guru’—has followed Śabara faithfully in his detailed gloss called Bṛhatī. His school has become known as Bhāṭṭamata or Gurumata.
There is a sub-commentary on this Bṛhatī by one Śālikanātha Miśra, known as Ṛjuvimālā.
Practically nothing is known of him. Tradition holds that he was a pupil of Kumārila.

pratinidhi
(‘one who represents another’)
------------------------------------------
In general, the word means a person who can act on behalf of someone else; or a substitute in a rite.
The पूर्वमीमाṁसा system, while dealing with वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, is very definite that a प्रतिनिधि or substitute is not allowed with regard to the devatā (deity), the five Vedic fires, the particular मन्त्र to be chanted on a particular occasion, certain specially prescribed rites as also the svāmin (the sacrificer).
The Atrismṛti (verses 50 and 51) permits a person to perform Gaṅgāsnāna (bath in the river गङ्गा) vicariously by requesting another who is actually going on a पिल्ग्रिमगे, in case he himself is unable to do so due to old-age, disease or any other valid reason. This second person has to do it by immersing a doll made of कुश grass in the river with appropriate mantras. This doll then becomes a ‘prati-nidhi’ of the first person who is unable to perform the पिल्ग्रिमगे.

Praṇava
(‘that by which [God] is effectively praised,’ ‘that which is ever new’)
------------------------------------------
Praṇava or Om is the universally accepted symbol of हिन्दुइस्म्. All sections, cults and groups honour this and use this. Even जैनिस्म्, बुद्धिस्म् and सिखिस्म् have adopted this. It is both an auricular and a visual symbol for ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute of Hindu philosophy, and God of Hindu religion.
Literally the word ‘Praṇava’ means ‘that by which God is effectively praised’. It also means ‘that which is ever new’. The word ‘Om’ is derived from the Sanskrit root ‘ava’ which has nineteen different senses. From these it is possible to construe that Om represents that Power which
is omniscient;
rules over the entire universe;
protects one from the evils of life;
fulfills the cherished desires of its devotees; and,
destroys इग्नोरन्चे and gives enlightenment.
Praṇava has been extolled highly in the वेदस्, the उपनिषद्स् and the Gītā as also in other scriptures. The Gopatha-brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda relates a story according to which god इन्द्र successfully overcame the demons with the help of Om. The story can be interpreted to mean that man can conquer his beastly nature by having recourse to the repetition of Om. The Yajurveda exhorts us to try to realise ब्रह्मन् through repeating and remembering Om. The Kaṭhopaniṣad declares that Om is परब्रह्मन् itself. The Muṇḍakopaniṣad advises the spiritual aspirant to meditate on the unity of the आत्मन् (the Self) with ब्रह्मन् (God) using Om for जप. Śrī कृष्ण avers in the Gītā that he is Om among words and that all religious rites are started with the repetition of Om. Not only that, if anyone succeeds in reciting the word Om at the time of his death, simultaneously thinking of God, he will attain the highest Truth. The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि declares that प्रणव is the symbol of God and that one can get समाधि on him by its repetition, and meditation of him.
Actually Om comprises three independent letters a, u and m, each of which has its own meaning and significance. The letter ‘a’ represents ‘beginning’ (ādimatva); ‘u’ represents ‘progress’ (utkarṣa); ‘m’ represents ‘limit or dissolution’ (miti). Hence the word Om represents that power responsible for च्रेअतिओन्, development and dissolution of this universe, i.e., God Himself.
Svāmi Vivekānanda has given a very simple but interesting and instructive explanation of the three letters comprising Om thereby bringing out the uniqueness of this great symbol: ‘The first letter A is the root-sound, the key, pronounced without touching any part of the tongue or the palate; M represents the last sound in the series, being produced by closed lips; and the U rolls from the very root to the end of the sounding-board of the mouth. Thus Om represents the whole phenomenon of sound-producing. As such it must be the natural symbol, the matrix of all the various sounds. It denotes the whole range, and possibility of all the words that can be made.’
The full significance of this statement becomes unfolded only when we understand the Hindu theory of च्रेअतिओन् as mentioned in the वेदस् and other scriptures. This theory can be summed up as follows:
Creation is not a linear process, beginning and ending at particular points of time, but it is a cyclic process going on eternally;
God creates this universe out of Himself by Himself. To put it in a technical language, He is both the material cause and the efficient cause;
Before beginning any particular cycle of च्रेअतिओन्, He utters the Vedic words denoting the various classes of beings and objects, conceives of the corresponding forms (remembering them from the previous cycles of च्रेअतिओन्) and creates them.
Contrary to the general understanding, this means that forms (rūpa) are preceded by names (nāma). Names are composed of letters which are sounds. All sounds are included in Om. Hence, the entire च्रेअतिओन् which proceeds from Vedic words or sounds, proceeds from the basic matrix of all sounds, viz., Om. Since God is the origin of this universe Om and God are identical. Or, at least, Om is the best symbol of God.
God is one. Sages call Him by various names. Though these various names differ from one another, all of them have sprung from the same basic source of all sounds, viz., Om. Hence Om represents all names of God; or, it is the best name of God.

Prādeśamātra
(‘of the dimension of prādeśa’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term specially used in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.18.1) to indicate ईश्वर or God who is the Self of all. The Upaniṣad has used the word ‘Vaiśvānarātman’ to indicate ईश्वर and calls him ‘Prādeśamātra’.
The word ‘prādeśa’ means space. He whose prādeśa extends from the dyuloka (heaven) as the head and the पृथ्वी (earth) as the feet is ‘Prādeśamātra’.
The word may also mean the Self within, who enjoys the ड़ोओद् that is eaten through the mouth.

Prajāpati
(‘Lord of beings’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘Prajāpati’ has been widely used in the Vedic literature, the उपनिषद्स्, the epics and the पुराणस्.
Literally, the word means ‘one who is the Lord of living beings.’ It was first used for the four-faced ब्रह्मा, the creator. Later on, it was used to indicate the nine mānasaputras or मिन्द्-born sons of ब्रह्मा like कर्दम, मरीचि, Aṅgirasa, दक्ष and others, who were also great sages.
In the उपनिषद्स् he is shown as a teacher of spiritual wisdom (vide, Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2).
The Bhagavadgītā (3.10-12) describes him as giving special instructions to the gods and the human beings after creating them and यज्ञ or sacrifice as a link between them.

Praśna Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This Upaniṣad has been assigned by tradition to the Atharvaveda. The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad which also belongs to the same Veda, has been called ‘Mantra’ and this Upaniṣad as ‘Brāhmaṇa’ by शङ्कर (A.

-820).
Considered as an ancient and authoritative scripture, it has been listed among the ten major उपनिषद्स्. Since it is in the form of six questions and their answers, it is called ‘Praśnopaniṣad’ or even ‘Ṣaṭpraśnopaniṣad’. The total number of verses, all in prose, is 67.
First Chapter (16 verses)
Six sages, all devoted to Brahman—Sukeśā, Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇi, Kausalya, भार्गव and Kabandhī—once approached the venerable sage पिप्पलाद, with the sacrificial fuel in hand (as per the prescribed traditional mode of approaching the spiritual teacher) and expressed their desire to know ब्रह्मन् from him. पिप्पलाद advised them to live in his होउसे for a year, doing तपस् or austerity and observing ब्रह्मचर्य (all the disciplines of studenthood). After completing their probation, they could approach him with their questions and doubts.
Having complied with his directions, they returned to him. Kabandhī was the first to ask: ‘O Venerable one! From where are all these creatures born?’
Pippalāda’s reply may be summarised as follows: प्रजापति, the Lord of च्रेअतिओन्, desirous of offspring, performed तपस् (austerity in the form of intense concentration on the process of च्रेअतिओन् as done in his previous existence) and brought out (of himself) a pair, the rayi and the प्राण, which pair would produce the creatures on his behalf.
Rayi is matter and प्राण is the sentient spirit. Rayi is identified with the मोओन् and प्राण with the sun. The sun and the मोओन् together are also responsible for the concept of time.
After briefly narrating च्रेअतिओन्, पिप्पलाद describes the two paths—the उत्तरायण and the Dakṣiṇāyana—by which human beings go to the higher worlds in accordance with their deeds. Those who are devoted to इष्टापूर्त (Vedic rituals like the अग्निहोत्र and public utility works like digging wells) will go to the पितृलोक (the world of manes) by the latter path. However they have to return to this world after exhausting their religious merit. Others devoted to तपस् (austerity), ब्रह्मचर्य (continence) and विद्या (contemplation on the deities) will go to the Ādityaloka (the world of the sun) by the former and will not return to this mundane existence.
Continuing his discourse, पिप्पलाद compares the saṁvatsara (the year with its two parts, the southern and the northern solstices), the month (with its dark and bright fortnights) and the day (with its day and night divisions) to Prjāpati. Even अन्न or ड़ोओद् is प्रजापति, because, it is out of the semen, the product of ड़ोओद्, that people are born; and, प्रजापति is the origin of all beings.
Second Chapter (13 verses)
The Second praśna (= question) or chapter starts with the question of भार्गव: Sir, how many देवस् (gods) are supporting this body? Who is illumining it? Among them who is the best?
In reply पिप्पलाद declares that it is प्राण that is actually supporting the body. He narrates a brief story as to how the sense-organs like the eye or the ear claimed superiority but were silenced. When the enraged प्राण moved as if he was getting up, all the other organs too were forced to rise up from their locations. It was like the queen bee rising, forcing all the ordinary bees also to rise. Then all the senses, understanding प्राण’s superiority started hymning to him. In this hymn, प्राण has been praised not just as the Self, the master of the body, but as the Supreme Self, प्रजापति himself. He is fire, sun, rain, इन्द्र, वायु, the earth, in fact, the Supreme God. He is परमेश्वर or रुद्र. He it is that receives all oblations given in sacrifices. In this body, it is he who functions as the sense-organs.
They request him to protect them even as a मोथेर् protects her children.
Third Chapter (12 Verses)
Now, it is the turn of Kausalya to question पिप्पलाद. His question concerns the प्राण or the vital energy working inside the body. His questions are: Whence is this प्राण born? How does he come into this body? How does he distribute himself and establish himself? In what way does he depart? How does he support the external world? How does he support what is inside oneself?
In the previous section though प्राण’s nature and greatness were described, his essential nature as the highest truth and his functions were not. They are now being delineated.
The प्राण is born or manifested from the आत्मन् (Paramapuruṣa or the Supreme Being). He comes into the body effortlessly like a shadow following a man, when the jīvātman (the individual Self) enters it. He appoints the five functional prāṇas (his own different aspects or parts) even as a king appoints his officers and apportions their duties. The five prāṇas are: प्राण (secondary), अपान, व्यान, उदान and समान. Their respective functions are: breathing and activating the eyes and the ears; excretion; general diffusing of the air inside the body; taking the jīvātman out of the body at the time of death; equitable distribution of the essence of ड़ोओद् all over the body.
There are 101 nāḍīs (tube-like structures for the flow of prāṇic energy) in the region of the heart. The उदान takes the jīvātman through one of them, the सुषुम्ना, to either meritorious worlds or हेल्ल् or back to the human world, depending on the कर्म of that individual—whether good or bad or mixed.
Āditya or the sun is the external aspect of प्राण who is also supporting the power of the eye inside. The earth, the sky, the light (outside) and the air (outside) are the external aspects respectively of अपान, समान, उदान and व्यान.
At the time of death, in whatever way the मिन्द् (of the dying person) works, the (chief) प्राण takes him to the world appropriate to him.
The section concludes with a eulogy of the person who has mastered the knowledge of this प्राण.
Fourth Chapter (11 verses)
Now Sauryāyaṇi questions पिप्पलाद: In this पुरुष (or body) what is it that sleeps? What is awake? Between these two, who sees the द्रेअम्स्? Who enjoys happiness? In whom are all united and dissolved?
When the sense-organs with their experiences become one with the मिन्द्, a person is said to be sleeping. Even then, the five prāṇas (compared to the five Vedic fires like गार्हपत्य by the Upaniṣad) are fully awake since they continue to function under the general guidance of the मिन्द्. It is this मिन्द् (or the jīvātman, the individual Self closely associated with it) that gets all the dream experiences.
However, when this मिन्द् (or the jīvātman) with the senses withdrawn into itself is merged in ब्रह्मन् (in deep sleep), there are no द्रेअम्स्. On the other hand, there is an experience of happiness. It is like the birds coming back in the evening to the tree where they live and be at peace. Thus, it is into ब्रह्मन् (or परमात्मन्, the Supreme Self) that all get united and dissolved.
The section ends with the eulogy that one who realises this truth becomes one with all.
Fifth Chapter (7 verses)
Then Satyakāma steps in to put the question: ‘What world does a human being, who has been meditating on ओङ्कार throughout his life, even until death, gain?’
Pippalāda now discourses on the significance of प्रणव or ओङ्कार, the method of meditating on it and the consequent fruits attained.
Oṅkāra is (i.e., can be a symbol for) both परब्रह्मन् and Aparabrahman, the unmanifested and the manifested aspects. Hence one can choose it as a symbol for meditation on either of these aspects.
Om has three parts, syllables, called ‘mātras’: a, u and m. One who meditates on ब्रह्मन् through the first syllable ‘a,’ attains a human birth that is conducive to a life of तपस् (austerity) and ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy). If he meditates through the second syllable ‘u,’ he is reborn in the world of सोम or मोओन्. After enjoying विभूति (wealth and intense pleasures) there, he will return to the human world. But one who meditates on the third syllable, ‘m,’ will be freed from all sins, will go to ब्रह्मलोक, the abode of ब्रह्मन् and will not return to mundane existence.
Some commentators have interpreted the word ‘mātrā’ in the original not as ‘syllable’, but as a unit of time. According to them, one who chants Om for one unit of time—say, for instance, one second—will go to the world of men, for two units of time, to the world of मोओन् and for three units, to ब्रह्मलोक. This of course applies to each repetition. And it must be accompanied by meditation on ब्रह्मन्.
Sixth Chapter (8 Verses)
Once, Hiraṇyanābha, the prince of कोसल had asked Sukeśā the question, ‘Do you know the Ṣoḍaśakala पुरुष (the person with 16 aspects)?’ But he did not know the answer. Now Sukeśā is asking पिप्पलाद the same question.
Pippalāda replies that this पुरुष is in one’s own body. He is the आत्मन्. He is the creator.
He first created प्राण or हिरण्यगर्भ, the primary Person (also called सूत्रात्मन्) the totality of subtle च्रेअतिओन्. From this latter प्राण, these others were evolved: श्रद्धा (faith), आकाश (ether or sky), वायु (air), jyoti (light or fire), āpas (water), पृथ्वी (earth), indriya (sense organs), मनस् (mind), अन्न (food), vīrya (strength of body), तपस् (austerity), mantras (Vedas), कर्म (Vedic rituals), lokas (the various worlds) and nāma (names of objects in च्रेअतिओन्).
All these aspects of च्रेअतिओन् depend on the पुरुष even as the spokes in a wheel, on its hub.
At the time of dissolution of the world all these get merged in the पुरुष, even as the rivers merge in the ocean.
The six sages then worshipped Pippa-lāda as their गुरु and returned to their homes.

pratyabhijñā
(‘knowledge [got by] facing [it]’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used by काश्मीर् शैविस्म्.
When we see a person whom we had seen earlier—maybe, in a different place and circumstances—we recognise him as ‘He is that person’.
Īśvara (God) and the जीव (the individual सोउल्) are similar in nature. They both have ज्ञानशक्ति and क्रियाशक्ति (the power to know and act). This is known from the scriptures and the teachings of the spiritual preceptors.
Keeping this in मिन्द्, when the sādhaka (one who is practising spiritual disciplines) meditates on ईश्वर, he gradually destroys or overcomes māyā (ignorance as the veil) and realises or recognises that he is the same as ईश्वर. This is प्रत्यभिज्ञा.

Prapannagītā
------------------------------------------
Imitation has been a natural characteristic of human beings. The Bhagavad-gītā of the great epic Mahābhārata (Bhīṣmaparva 25-42)—more popularly known as the Gītā—has given rise to many other tracts of various lengths composed in verse form, to which the appellation Gītā is given.
Sixteen of such Gītās are from the Mahābhārata, twenty from various पुराणस् and four found as independent works untraced to any other known epic or purāṇa.
The Prapannagītā—also called the Pāṇḍavagītā—belongs to the last group.
There are eighty verses in different metres. They contain prayers addressed to कृष्ण as विष्णु-नारायण, the sentiment of प्रपत्ति (surrender to God) being predominant. Hence the title Prapannagītā (prapanna = one who has surrendered to God) is very apt.
The number of bhāgavatas or devotees of God whose prayers are included here exceeds sixty! Apart from the five Pāṇḍavas and a few persons prominent in the Mahābhārata like भीष्म, Droṇa and विदुर, many important sages figure in this work. Some of them are अगस्त्य, धौम्य, नारद, विश्वामित्र, जमदग्नि, भरद्वाज, गौतम, अत्रि, वसिष्ठ, कश्यप, भृगु, पराशर, व्यास and शुक.
The subjects dealt with are, briefly, as follows:
Homage to the great devotees like प्रह्लाद, Puṇḍarīka, शौनक, भीष्म, नारद and others; verses in praise of the five Pāṇḍavas who were great devotees of कृष्ण; description of the physical beauty of the Lord विष्णु-नारायण; prayer for devotion; various names of the Lord; obeisance to Him; devoted meditation on the Lord is superior to all religious acts; power of the divine name.

pratyāmnāya
(‘restatement,’ ‘that which comes in its place’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical word used in two senses.
In लोगिच्, it is used in the sense of re-asserting the प्रतिज्ञा or the original statement when the same is doubted or objected to.
In the धर्मशास्त्रस् it is used to indicate a substitute when the original rite cannot be done. For instance, when a particular expiation cannot be performed by the transgressor, another—a simpler or easier one—is prescribed. If the sinner is unable to donate a cow as expiation for a sin, he is permitted to pay some gold coins as prescribed. This is called प्रत्याम्नाय.

Praśastapāda
------------------------------------------
The Vaiśeṣikasūtras of कणाद or Aulūkya (who preceded बुद्ध) has a commentary called Praśastapādabhāṣya or Padārthadharmasaṅgraha by Praśasta-pāda. This commentary is more like a long independent essay on the Vaiśeṣika-sūtras than a regular bhāṣya. Apart from explaining the several terms and concepts of the sūtras, it has also brought in other doctrines like those of च्रेअतिओन्, dissolution, number, atoms in a molecule and transformation of colours by heat and so on, which do not find a place in the original.
Praśastapāda was the earliest writer on the Vaiśeṣikasūtras after कणाद and must have lived in the 5th or the 6th centuries A. D.

pratiloma
(‘against hair or grain’)
------------------------------------------
See ANULOMA.

pradhāna
(‘the chief one’)
------------------------------------------
See SĀṄKHYA DARŚANA.

prapatti
(‘total surrender [to God]’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term specially used in Rāmānuja’s (A.

-1137) philosophy (Viśiṣṭādvaita) and religion (Śrīvaiṣṇavism).
God-realisation is the final or the only goal of life. This again, is possible only through the path of भक्ति or devotion.
This path of भक्ति has two aspects: भक्तियोग and प्रपत्ति or Prapattiyoga.
Though the path of भक्ति or devotion to God ( = भक्तियोग) has been considered as easy, as compared to other yogas like ज्ञानयोग, it too has quite a few formal rules and disciplines to be followed. This naturally makes it a difficult path, especi-ally for the ordinary sādhakas who have neither the time nor the competence to observe these disciplines properly.
Here comes the role of the second path, that of प्रपत्ति or total surrender, complete submission to the will of God.
Prapatti is also known by other names such as आत्मसमर्पण, bhara-न्यास, nikṣepa, न्यास, prapadana and शरणागति. The meanings of all these terms are, more or less, the same.
The path of प्रपत्ति has the support of the scriptures, both the śrutis and the smṛtis (vide Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18; Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad 24.1; Bhagavad-gītā 2.7 and 18.66).
The practice of प्रपत्ति is of three types: svaniṣṭhā (depending upon oneself); uktiniṣṭhā (depending upon the आचार्य’s words or teachings); and, ācāryaniṣṭhā (giving the entire responsibility to the आचार्य or the spiritual teacher).
Prapatti has six steps. They are:
Making up one’s मिन्द् to follow the path approved by God and his great devotees (as revealed in the holy books).
Eschewing the path of evil that goes against the will of God and spiritual evolution.
Tremendous faith in God that he will certainly protect the surrendered person.
Hence, voluntarily and willingly choosing God alone as one’s protector.
Self-oblation or mentally keeping oneself at the feet of God for protection.
A sense of utter unworthiness of oneself vis-a-vis the task of attaining लिबेरतिओन्.
The following persons are unfit even for प्रपत्ति: those who are
unable to follow the prescribed disciplines;
devoid of faith in the आचार्य or teacher;
not willing to serve the गुरु or spiritual preceptor; and,
lacking faith in God.
The Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā (3
) and 28) as also the Rahasyatrayasāra (ch. 21) of वेदान्त देशिक (A.

-1369) deal with this subject.
One of the oft-quoted examples of प्रपत्ति is that of विभीषण in the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि (vide Yuddhakāṇḍa, chs. 17.17; 18.3; 18.33,34).
The cardinal principle in the doctrine of प्रपत्ति is that मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् depends entirely on God’s grace and not on the efforts of the sādhaka or the spiritual aspirant. Whereas there are limitations to human efforts, no such limitation exists for God’s grace!

praśvāsa
(‘exhalation’)
------------------------------------------
The words श्वास and प्रश्वास have been used by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his Yogasūtras (2.49) in connection with the definition of प्राणायाम. श्वास is inhalation and प्रश्वास is exhalation. They are also called पूरक and रेचक. When their movement is stopped temporarily, it results in प्राणायाम.
See also PRĀṆĀYĀMA.

pratijñā
(‘statement of assurance or assertion’)
------------------------------------------
The general meaning of the word is ‘giving word,’ ‘asserting something as true,’ ‘a statement of fact’.
However, in the Nyāyadarśana (Hindu लोगिच्) it is the first of the five steps of a logical statement.
Pratijñā is a statement of fact, as asserted by one who is ready to prove it.
For instance: ‘parvato vahnimān,’ ‘there is fire on the hill.’
This is subsequently proved by four steps: हेतु (reason); udāharaṇa (instance, example); upanaya (application of the general to the particular) and निगमन (final conclusion).

pradoṣa
(‘that which is full of दोष or defect’)
------------------------------------------
Any religious act should take into consideration the purpose as also the time and place before it is undertaken.
In this, kāla or time is a very important factor. Certain periods of time are considered as auspicious and certain others, inauspicious. One of these is प्रदोष.
It is the period of six ghaṭikās after sunset (1 ghaṭikā = 24 minutes). Some authorities reduce it to three ghaṭikās also.
Though generally this is considered as inauspicious—say, for the study of the scriptures—it is specially recommended for taking ड़ोओद् by one who is observing the vow of नक्त; i.e., eating once only in the day, and that too, at night. This applies to one observing एकादशी as a vrata or ड़स्तिन्ग् as an expiation.
See also EKĀDAŚĪ.

praṇītā
(‘fetched [water]’)
------------------------------------------
In the दर्शपूर्णमास sacrifice, पुरोडाश cakes (of rice or barley grains) are offered. The water that is used for preparing the dough has to be brought in a चमस (wooden cup with a handle) purified with pavitras (or दर्भ grass), from the north of the गार्हपत्य fire to the north of the आहवनीय fire, to the accompaniment of certain mantras (vide Taittirīya Saṁhitā
.1). This process is called praṇītāpraṇayana and the waters as प्रणीता.

pratimā
(‘icon,’ ‘image’)
------------------------------------------
See MŪRTIŚILPAŚĀSTRA.

pratiyogi
(‘that which is the opposite’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in philosophical systems like the Vaiśeṣika (of the sage कणाद) where अभाव or non-existence of a thing is also considered as a पदार्थ or category.
In a particular place (which is empty) there is no घट or pot. Hence we should accept that there is the अभाव (non-existence) of the घट. The opposite of this ghaṭābhāva (absence of the pot) is the pot, which is brought and kept there. Once this is done, the ghaṭābhāva disappears. Hence the pot is called the ‘pratiyogi’ of the absence of the pot.

prastara
(‘that which is strewn’)
------------------------------------------
In वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, since even the implements used are considered sacred, they should be kept on the वेदि (platform) in a clean and pure place. Whereas cleanliness is external and physical, purity is more a ceremonial concept.
Before placing the sruk and sruva (offering ladles) on the वेदि, a small bundle of दर्भ grass (Poa cynosuroides) is spread out first. The ladles are then placed on this bundle which is called प्रस्तर.

prāṇāyāma
(‘controlling of प्राण’)
------------------------------------------
Prāṇa is the cosmic energy or life-force which is permeating not only the inanimate universe but also all the living beings.
The Hindu sages had discovered even from the most ancient times, the techniques of controlling and channelising this life-force and put it to various uses.
This science of controlling प्राण is known as प्राणायाम.
The word ‘prāṇāyāma’ has been defined as lengthening or dispersing the prāṇic energy so as to pervade the whole body in a uniform manner.
The subject of प्राणायाम has been dealt with not only in राजयोग (vide पतञ्जलि’s Yogasūtras 2.49-53) but also in हठयोग (vide Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā 5; Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.71-77).
In राजयोग, it is listed as the fourth of the eight steps of योग leading to समाधि (the last step).
Since there is an intimate connection between the मिन्द् and the प्राण, which again, can be regulated through the regulation of the breathing process, the मिन्द् can be brought under control by controlling breath. This is the philosophy behind प्राणायाम as given in the Yoga-sūtras.
In this work, प्राणायाम is described as having three steps: पूरक (inhalation), कुम्भक (retention of breath) and रेचक (exhalation).
Air has to be inhaled through the left nostril, should be retained in the lungs for some time and then exhaled through the right nostril. The same process should then be repeated in the reverse order. This forms one round of प्राणायाम proper.
The relative proportion, with regard to time, can be 1:4:2; or 1:2:2; or 1:1:1. In other words, if पूरक or inhalation is done, say, in 8 seconds, कुम्भक or retention must be for (8 x 4 =) 32 seconds and रेचक or exhalation, for (8 x 2 =) 16 seconds.
This प्राणायाम is regulated by three factors: deśa (distance of air measured during exhalation), kāla (time taken for each of the three processes like 4 seconds: 16 seconds: 8 seconds) and saṅkhyā (the number of prāṇāyāmas per sitting). These should be gradually increased until the following limits are reached, if possible: 24 to 36 inches; 16:64:8; 80 per sitting and 320 per day.
However, these limits are for extra-ordinary and highly qualified sādhakas who practise it under the direct guidance of an expert गुरु. Hence it should never be attempted by others.
This threefold प्राणायाम must be preceded by what is called नाडीशुद्धि. In this exercise, only the पूरक and रेचक are practised without कुम्भक.
The works on हठयोग describe not only various kinds of prāṇāyāmas but also various avasthās or stages involved. They also predicate various kinds of phalas or fruits resulting from their practice like getting rid of sins and curing of ailments.
Prāṇāyāma being a highly complicated process fraught with serious consequences if wrongly done, should be practised only under the direct guidance of adepts in the field. Several preconditions like purity of physical and ethical life, should also be strictly adhered to.

pratīkopāsanā
(‘meditation on a symbol’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word upāsanā literally means ‘sitting near (God)’, it is always used in the sense of worship or meditation.
Hinduism posits मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence as the final goal of life (called परमपुरुषार्थ).
There are two royal paths leading to this: the path of ज्ञान (knowledge) and the path of भक्ति (devotion), also called ज्ञानयोग and भक्तियोग respectively.
In both these paths upāsanā has an important place.
In the ज्ञानयोग, the upāsanā has to be on the आत्मन् (the Self within) which is nirākāra (formless) and nirguṇa (without any attribute), but whose essence is sat-cit-आनन्द (existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss). Since this upāsanā or meditation is extremely difficult for the beginners or the ordinary aspirants, a pratīka or a symbol like प्रणव (Oṁ, the sound), सूर्य (the sun), आकाश (space), अग्नि (fire) and so on, is chosen for meditation.
For those who find even this as a difficult path, भक्तियोग recommends meditation on the images of gods or goddesses. Here, the image is not considered God, but only as an aid to imagine in one’s own heart, God as a being of light and चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, lovingly responding to one’s prayers.
Such meditations come under the category of प्रतीकोपासना.

prāṇāgnihotra
(‘[act of eating] compared to अग्निहोत्र to satisfy the prāṇas’)
------------------------------------------
The कर्मकाण्ड of the वेदस् is full of not only the instructions about sacrifices but also contains their eulogy.
In the आरण्यकस् and the उपनिषद्स्, however, there is a tendency to minimise their ritualistic aspects and substitute them with subtle mental ideas, sometimes associated with ordinary acts of day-to-day life also. The प्राणाग्निहोत्र of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.19-24) is one such instance. Here the act of eating has been elevated to the level of the अग्निहोत्र, a daily sacrifice.
According to the instructions given in the Upaniṣad, the first five morsels of ड़ोओद् are to be preceded by the following mantras: prāṇāya स्वाहा; vyānāya स्वाहा; apānāya स्वाहा; samānāya स्वाहा; udānāya स्वाहा.
When these five prāṇas are satisfied by these ritual offerings, they produce certain special results like progeny, possession of cows and excellent physical characteristics, including smooth functioning of the senses.

pratipattikarma
(‘action done intentionally’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in various senses.
The most general sense is abandoning something after its use is over. For instance, when an आहिताग्नि (one who has established Vedic fires) dies, all the wooden vessels and implements he was using in performing sacrifices, are disposed off, by keeping them on the various parts of his body during its च्रेमतिओन् (vide the Pūrvamīmāṁsāsūtras (1

prakṛtilaya
(‘dissolution into the प्रकृति’)
------------------------------------------
In the Sāṅkhya and the योग systems, out of the several attainments predicated for the sādhakas (or aspirants of योग), the state of प्रकृतिलय is also one.
Some practitioners of योग, who have developed intense वैराग्य or detachment towards the world and its pleasures, but who have not acquired the right type of विवेक or discriminatory knowledge, meditate on the प्रकृति (or प्रधान), the fundamental matrix of the material universe. By समाधि on it, they are able to merge themselves in it after death. This state called ‘prakṛtilaya,’ though free from sorrow, is devoid of any चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् or bliss. After being in this condition for a very long time, they return to सṁसार or transmigratory existence, the cycle of births and deaths.
The Sāṅkhyasūtras (45) of ईश्वर-कृष्ण (4th cent. A. D.) and the Yogasūtras (1.19) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) refer to this state.

prakāra
(‘mode’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in some philosophical works of न्याय (logic) and Mīmāṁsā (Vedic ritualism).
A प्रकार is that which distinguishes something from the common group. For instance, द्रव्य or a substance is stated to be of nine types. पृथ्वी (earth), one of them, is a प्रकार or mode of that द्रव्य.
In the phrase ‘daṇḍavān puruṣaḥ’ (the person with the stick) दण्ड or stick is the प्रकार or mode that distinguishes him from others.
Implication and similarity are other senses in which the word is used.

prārabdhakarma
(‘karma that has started giving the results’)
------------------------------------------
The doctrine of karma—that कर्म or action done in any life must produce its result, good or bad, now or in future (including future births)—is a fundamental belief in हिन्दुइस्म्.
Of the three karmas recognised (See KARMA for details.) the prārabdha कर्म is the second. It simply means the कर्म that has started giving its fruits by causing the present birth.

Pratāparudra Deva
------------------------------------------
A descendant of the Sūryavaṁśa (the Solar race), प्रतापरुद्र देव was the king of Orissa from A.
to 1540. Though a valiant king, he was deeply influenced by श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A.

-1533) and became his initiated disciple. As a result, he neglected the affairs of the State and started spending most of his time in spiritual pursuits. Under his patronage, the Oriya language developed remarkably well. Several works on भक्ति or devotion to कृष्ण were composed in his time.
See also ŚRĪKṚṢṆACAITANYA.

Pradyumna
------------------------------------------
Pradyumna was a reincarnation of मन्मथ (the god of love, Cupid). He was born as the son of कृष्ण and रुक्मिणी. He was considered as a partial manifestation of the sage Sanatkumāra.
As soon as he was born, the demon शम्बरासुर is said to have abducted him and thrown him into the sea, where a big fish swallowed him. The fishermen who caught it brought it to the palace kitchen of Śambara. The cooks, on cutting it found a baby inside it! This baby was then adopted by Māyāvatī, the chief maid of Śambara’s queen and brought him up. She was actually रति, मन्मथ’s queen in disguise. Later on प्रद्युम्न killed Śambara and married Māyāvatī.
He is said to have died during the infighting among the Yādavas.
See also CATURVYŪHAS.

pratibimbavāda
(‘the doctrine [that the] जीव is a reflection [of ब्रह्मन्]’)
------------------------------------------
See ADVAITA VEDĀNTA DARŚANA.

Prārthanā Samāj
------------------------------------------
During the eighteenth and the nineteenth centuries, India witnessed several Hindu revival and reform movements. Though generally rooted in the ancient value-system, they tried to give Hindu religion and society a modern look, in consonance with the changing ethos brought about by the British conquest of India and an invasion of Western culture.
One such movement of these times is the प्रार्थना समाज् of Bombay (now Mumbai). Inspired by the visits of केशवचन्द्र सेन् (A.
-1884), Dr. Ātmārām Pāṇḍuraṅg (A.
-1898) started it in 1867. R. G. Bhaṇḍārkar (A.
-1925) and M. G. Rānaḍe (A.

-1901) were the main leaders of this movement.
Though inspired by the Brāhmo movement of Bengal, the प्रार्थना समाज् did not go to the extent of alienating itself from the traditional Hindu religion and society. It remained more like a protestant movement within हिन्दुइस्म्.
A positive belief in the unity of God, a great stress on the abandonment of caste, introduction of remarriage of widows, encouragement of female एदुचतिओन्, and the abolition of the purdah system as also child मर्रिअगे were the main tenets and programmes of this Samāj.
It drew its inspiration largely from the Hindu scriptures and the songs of Marāṭhi mystical poets.
The movement did not spread beyond the Mahārāṣṭra region and gradually faded out.

prājña
(‘one who knows well’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedānta philosophy, based mainly on the उपनिषद्स्, has utilised the technique of avasthātrayaviveka—an analysis of the three states of consciousness—for proving the existence of a conscious सोउल् (the jīvātman or the आत्मन्) as separate from the body-मिन्द् complex. (See AVASTHĀTRAYA for details.)
The three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् are: जाग्रत् (the waking state), स्वप्न (the dream state) and the सुषुप्ति (the deep-sleep state).
The jīvātman as associated with these three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is respectively known as viśva, तैजस and प्राज्ञ.
In the जाग्रत् state, the jīvātman identifies himself with the physical body as also the मिन्द्. In the स्वप्न state, identification with the physical body is transcended but that with the मिन्द् still remains. In the सुषुप्ति state, even the मिन्द् is transcended and the jīvātman is aware of only himself and as a sākṣi or witness. It is in this state that he is called ‘prājña’.
He is designated as ‘prājña’ since prajñapti or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् is his only characteristic or form (‘prajñaptimātram’).
However, the Vedāntasāra of Sadā-नन्द (44) defines him as ‘prāyeṇa ajñaḥ.’ ‘He is ignorant to a great extent’ since his conscious nature is overcome by अज्ञान, by रजस् and तमस् (vide the commentary Vidvanmanorañjanī on the section 44).
See Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 9 to 11 for a description of these three states of the jīvātman.

pratigara
(‘response’)
------------------------------------------
A Vedic sacrifice involves several rites and minor rites including the chanting of certain classes of śastras (See ŚASTRA for details.).
The होतृ priest issues a call called आहाव (See also ĀHĀVA.) to which the अध्वर्यु priest responds by loudly uttering the प्रतिगर (reply or response).
There are several āhāvas for which there are appropriate pratigaras also.
For instance, for the आहाव, “Śoṁ 3 sāvo3m” (“Let us both praise!”), the (reply) प्रतिगर is “Othamo daivā” or “Śoṁsāmo daivā” (“Let us praise the deity!”).
In course of time the two seem to have acquired a mystical significance. Several permutations and combinations were evolved because of this.

pratyāhāra
(‘withdrawal [of the senses from outside] towards [oneself]’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the eight steps of योग as described by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) in his Yogasūtras (2.29).
See YOGADARŚANA for details.

pramāda
(‘heedlessness’)
------------------------------------------
In general, the word means heedlessness or carelessness and a blunder that arises out of it.
However, in the Yogasūtras (1.30) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) it is used as a technical term and listed as an obstacle to योग or समाधि. It is defined as neither remembering nor practising the basic virtues like अहिṁसा (non-injury) and सत्य (truth), which are essential for attaining समाधि.
Once the मिन्द् is allowed to slip from the path of योग due to प्रमाद, it can result in a total fall (vide Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, 324). The famous sage Sanatsujāta compares प्रमाद to मृत्यु or death since it ultimately leads to सṁसार or transmigratory existence (vide Sanatsujātīya 1.4).

prathamakalpika
------------------------------------------
According to the Vyāsabhāṣya on the Yogasūtras (3.51) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.), the yogis can be categorised into four groups: प्रथमकल्पिक; मधुभूमिक; प्रज्ञाज्योति; and अतिक्रान्तभावनीय. The प्रथमकल्पिक has just started the practice of योग. He has not had any experience.
The मधुभूमिक has got समाधि on the पञ्चभूतस् (elements) and the इन्द्रियस् (senses). He has succeeded in getting ऋतम्भरप्रज्ञा, the state of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् which gives the truth of everything that the योगि thinks of.
The प्रज्ञाज्योति is the third type of योगि who has conquered the sense-organs and the five elements and is very near to puruṣakhyāti or realisation of the आत्मन्, the Self.
The अतिक्रान्तभावनीय, the last, has attained the knowledge of the Self and hence a jīvanmukta, a liberated सोउल्.

pramathagaṇa
(‘the group of beings who punish [the evil ones]’)
------------------------------------------
Lord शिव is said to be surrounded by a very large retinue of godlings or semi-divine beings whose number is said to be 360 millions. They are capable of taking any form. Generally they appear like अस्चेतिच्स् with जटा (long matted hair) and ardha-चन्द्र (crescent मोओन्) on the hair. They are deeply devoted to शिव and spend their time in his service. They also fight on his behalf when necessary as on the occasion of destruction of दक्ष’s sacrifice.
Sometimes they are pictured more like horrible goblins.
They attack sinners and transgressors of धर्म, generally in the night.
However, good people who follow the dictates of धर्म, cannot come under their influence (vide Mahābhārata, Anuśāsanaparva 131).

prakṛti
(‘the natural or original principle,’ ‘that which produces effects’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the most widely used words in Sanskrit literature as also in the Hindu scriptures.
In the most basic sense, it means nature or a natural quality.
In वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्, it means a model yāga—like the Darśa or the Pūrṇamāsa—others based on it being called ‘vikṛtis’.
In grammar it represents the basic form of a word.
In the साङ्ख्य दर्शन, it represents प्रधान, the basic material cause of the universe, comprising the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्. This concept has generally been accepted by almost all the schools of Vedānta.
In Advaita Vedānta it stands for māyā at the cosmic level and अविद्या (ignorance) at the individual level.
In Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta it is called ‘acit’ (the unconscious principle) and accepted as a permanent reality, but under the control of ईश्वर or God.
The द्वैत Vedānta considers it as having two aspects: the citprakṛti (conscious entity same as लक्ष्मी, the divine consort of विष्णु) and the acitprakṛti or the unconscious basic material cause of the world.
In the Śāktatantras प्रकृति is the Divine मोथेर् who appears in five forms. They are: दुर्गा, राधा, लक्ष्मी, सरस्वती and सावित्री. These five goddesses are responsible for च्रेअतिओन्.
In the आयुर्वेद (health sciences) it stands for the general condition of the body.
The Bhagavadgītā (7.4, 5) describes प्रकृति as representing two aspects of the Lord’s power, the aparā (lower) and the parā (the higher). The former comprises eight unconscious material objects and the latter, the conscious जीव (individual सोउल्).
In political science (vide याज्ञवल्क्य Smṛti 1.353; कौटिल्य’s Arthaśāstra 6.1) the word stands for the seven राज्याङ्गस् or constituents of the state.
In Sanskrit poetry, it is the name of a particular metre with 21 letters or syllables per line.

Prajāpati Smṛti
------------------------------------------
The Smṛtis of बौधायन and वसिष्ठ as also the commentary Mitākṣarā on the Yajñavalkya Smṛti quote several verses from a Prajāpati Smṛti. Since most of these verses are found in the extant Manusmṛti and since मनु is sometimes counted among the Prajāpatis, it is likely that the word Prajāpati Smṛti may actually refer to the Manusmṛti only.
There is a printed edition bearing the title Prajāpati Smṛti containing 198 verses. However, the verses quoted in the works mentioned above do not figure in this work.
The topics attributed to प्रजापति in all these works or quotations are: śrāddha (obsequial rites); references to some of the signs of the zodiac like कन्या and Vṛścika; अशौच (ceremonial impurity); prāyaścittas (expiations for sins); on parivrājakas (saṁnyāsins or मोन्क्स्); witnesses and their reliability in disputes; rights of a sonless widow to succeed to her husband’s property as also to offer śrāddha and so on.

Prayāga
(‘[place of] excellent sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
Visiting places of pilgrimage—especially the important ones—at least once in life-time, has been prescribed as a sacred duty for every Hindu by the धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस्.
Holy dip at Triveṇi SaṅgamOne of the very few pilgrim centres, a visit to which has been considered extremely auspicious, is प्रयाग (the modern Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh). It has been designated as ‘Tīrtharāja’ (‘the king of पिल्ग्रिमगे centres’) also. Since the three rivers गङ्गा, यमुना and सरस्वती (the mythical river supposed to join the other two from underground) merge here, the place is also called ‘Triveṇī’. The actual confluence is known as त्रिवेणी saṅgama and is 2.4 kms. (1.5 miles) from the city.
Brahmā (the four-faced creator of the world) is said to have performed a याग or sacrifice here, which was the best (= pra or prakṛṣṭa) of all sacrifices. Hence the name प्रयाग.
Sometimes it is described as the madhyavedi, the middle altar, out of the five used by ब्रह्मा, the other four being कुरुक्षेत्र (in Haryana), गया (in Bihar), Virajā (somewhere in South India) and पुष्कर (in Rajasthan).
Some of the पुराणस् like the Matsya (

) declare that प्रयाग is not destroyed even in प्रलय or dissolution of the world.
The hoary antiquity of प्रयाग seems to be confirmed by a verse in the Ṛgveda itself (10.75, the खिल part), (See KHILA also.) though the Rāmāyaṇa (2. 54.6) refers to a forest at the place of the confluence of the two rivers.
Religious rites strongly recommended to be performed here are: bath at the त्रिवेणी-saṅgama, tonsure of the head (sometimes recommended even for women as प्रायश्चित्त or expiation), performance of śrāddha to ancestors and दान (giving gifts).
Veṇīpradāna (offering two to four inches of their braid of hair into the confluence, by married women) is another rite which is popular among the pilgrims even today.
One of the best places prescribed for committing religious सुइचिदे (by persons who have realised the Self or who are very old or who are suffering from incurable diseases causing much suffering and so on) is प्रयाग. It is done by jumping into the river from the Akṣaya-vaṭa, the famous (and age-old) Banyan tree on its bank.
A bath in the त्रिवेणी, in the month of Māgha (generally in January), is considered as extremely auspicious. During this period, many pilgrims assemble on the banks of the rivers and camp there, sometimes for three to four weeks.
It is again during this month, once in twelve years, that the famous Kumbha-melā festival is held here. (See KUMBHA-MELĀ.) It is the biggest religious festival in the world, drawing more than thirty million people, including thousands of साधुस् (religious mendicants and leaders) who all manage a dip in the rivers within the time span of twenty four hours!
Other holy places here that are visited by the pilgrims are: Veṇīmādhava temple, Bharadvājāśrama, Nāgamandira (or Vāsukimandira) and the अक्षयवट.
The चित्रकूट hill of the Rāmāyaṇa-fame (vide Ayodhyākāṇḍa 56) is situated at a distance of about one hundred kilometers (60 miles) from here. (See CITRAKŪṬA for details.)
